Some (long) practical advice to you:

I wonder if an IT job is appropriate for someone whose depressive symptoms lead them to browsing on the internet for hours. That's what my depression is like, and I'm getting more done when I'm not on the computer. So I have a feeling IT might not be a good idea for you.

Have you spoken with a doctor regarding the depression? It's good if you have some documentation/backup if you want to make the case that you need a medical waiver.

Talk to your professors. See your counselors/academic advisors immediately and ask them what can be done. Explain your depression and medical situations. Ask about medical withdrawals, withdrawals that won't affect your GPA, and appeals that you could do after the grades have been assigned, if need be. Ask about doing "incompletes" for your courses so you can finish your work with a little extension. You can also look on your school's website to get an idea of the policies regarding these things. At some point soon (like now), you're going to have to make contact with someone.

Generally, they are willing to help. You may not like the final result, but they do help. I'm in a similar situation at the moment. They key is communicating with professors and advisors and documenting.

You should also ask your advisors about the job opportunities, btw. Maybe not now because you'll want to prioritize your grades, but soon. In my opinion, just because you failed a couple classes doesn't make you incompetent and doesn't mean you can't get a PhD. But you'll probably have to put in extra work elsewhere to compensate, lol. There are many stories of people who failed college then came back to complete the program but then even got a PhD at the same uni. Heard about a guy like this at my school. Very inspiring. Don't fail if you can help it, but know there are many routes to a particular destination.

I wouldn't necessarily give up on your career because of this. I can understand bleak job options, but make sure to consider that you might actually enjoy the job so much that it makes low pay worth it (live to work vs work to live?). Also, explore other branches of work you can do with your degree in the meantime, as an alternative to PhD (or something to do till you get there).
